summary: This paper studies the usage and importance of Linux APIs, including system calls, pseudo-files, and libc functions, across all applications and libraries in the Ubuntu 15.04 distribution. To achieve this, the authors combine static analysis of API usage with survey data to weight the relative importance of applications to end users. The study proposes metrics to evaluate the maturity of prototype systems or compatibility layers. It reports that many APIs are rarely used, some security-relevant API changes have seen slow adoption, and numerous libc interfaces are effectively unused, suggesting opportunities to improve system security and efficiency.

sections.title: 2.1 API Importance: A Metric for Individual APIs

highlights.quote: we define API importance as the probability that an API will be indis- pensable to at least one application on a randomly selected installation.
highlights.note: Defines the core proposed metric (API importance) used to solve the research problem.

highlights.quote: We want a metric that decreases as one identi- fies and removes instances of a deprecated API, and a metric that will remain high for an indispensable API, even if only one ubiquitous application uses the API.
highlights.note: Provides the justification for why this specific metric is designed this way and why it is expected to be effective.

highlights.quote: Definition: API Importance. For a given API, the probability that an installation in- cludes at least one application requiring the given API.
highlights.note: Introduces the 'API Importance' metric as a way to quantify the necessity of an API.

highlights.quote: Intuitively, if an API is used by no packages or installations, the API importance will be zero, causing no negative effects if removed.
highlights.note: Provides the justification for why this metric is useful for determining if an API can be removed without negative effects.

highlights.quote: We also measure compatibility at the granularity of an OS, which we call weighted completeness.
highlights.note: Introduces 'weighted completeness' as the proposed metric for measuring OS compatibility.

highlights.quote: Weighted complete- ness is the fraction of applications that are likely to work, weighted by the likelihood that these applications will be in- stalled on a system.
highlights.note: Describes how the proposed solution (weighted completeness) is constructed/defined.

highlights.quote: The goal of weighted completeness is to measure the degree to which a new OS prototype or translation layer is compatible with a baseline OS.
highlights.note: Explains the purpose and intended utility of the proposed metric.

highlights.quote: Weighted Completeness. For a target system, the fraction of applications sup- ported, weighted by the popularity of these applications.
highlights.note: Defines the proposed system-wide metric for measuring API support.

highlights.quote: The methodology for measuring the weighted complete- ness of a target system’s API subset is summarized as fol- lows: 1. Start with a list of supported APIs of the target system, either identified from the system’s source, or as provided by the developers of the system. 2. Based on the API footprints of packages, the framework generates a list of supported and unsupported packages. 3. The framework then considers the dependencies of pack- ages. If a supported package depends on an unsupported package, both packages are marked as unsupported. 4. Finally, the framework weighs the list of supported pack- ages based on package installation statistics.
highlights.note: Describes how the proposed solution (Weighted Completeness) is implemented/achieved.

highlights.quote: We implement a simple call-graph analysis to detect system calls reach- able from the binary entry point (e entry in ELF head- ers).
highlights.note: Describes a key component of the implementation to achieve the research goal.

highlights.quote: Our call-graph analysis allows us to only select system calls that are actually used by the application, not all the sys- tem calls that appear in libc.
highlights.note: Explains why the call-graph analysis is a superior method for identifying used system calls.

highlights.quote: Our analysis takes the following steps: • For a target executable or a library, generate a call graph of internal function usage. • For each library function that the executable relies on, identify the code in the library that is reachable from each entry point called by the executable. • For each library function that calls another library call, recursively trace the call graph and aggregate the results.
highlights.note: Details the step-by-step implementation of the proposed solution.

sections.title: A.2 Weighted Completeness — A System-Wide Metric

highlights.quote: Definition: Weighted Completeness. For a target system, the fraction of applications sup- ported, weighted by the popularity of these applications.
highlights.note: Defines the proposed metric 'Weighted Completeness' used to evaluate relative compatibility.

highlights.quote: Using weighted completeness, one can estimate the fraction of packages in an installation that end-users can expect a tar- get system to support.
highlights.note: Explains why the solution is believed to work/be useful: it provides an estimate of expected package support for end-users.
